routes.description: Establish that consciousness, a persisting personal subject, future-directed purpose, objective value, and genuine agency contain features that no exhaustive physical description can constitute or explain.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if at least one motion-level feature is shown to be real and indispensable to personhood while remaining neither identical with nor fully explicable through physical structure, computation, function, or causal history.

motionBridge.description: Show that one or more essential features of persons require an ontological or explanatory basis beyond an exhaustive inventory of physical facts.

centralBridges.description: Establish that first-person experience is a determinate fact whose existence and qualitative character are not exhausted by neural, behavioral, or functional descriptions.
Establish that unified experience, memory, anticipation, reasoning, and choice require a continuing subject that uses but is not identical with the brain.
Establish that intentional purposes, objective values, and controlled alternative possibilities have normative or causal roles unavailable to purposeless physical processes alone.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support irreducibility by distinguishing the brain's provision of access to consciousness from the production or exhaustive constitution of consciousness.
Require justification for treating an unfinished and conceptually unsettled naturalistic program as capable of explaining every feature named in the motion.

routes.description: Show that consciousness and personhood arise through evolved physical organization while purpose, value, identity, and responsible agency remain genuine at appropriate functional and higher explanatory levels.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic accounts accommodate the phenomena named in the motion without eliminating their practical significance and no additional nonphysical subject, property, purpose giver, or causal power is required.

motionBridge.description: Show that materially realized processes and legitimate higher-level explanations jointly account for persons without implying metaphysical ingredients beyond the natural world.

centralBridges.description: Explain conscious perspective and the apparent self through unconscious brain computation, responsiveness, and an evolved user interface without positing a separate inner observer.
Explain how purposeless evolution, prediction, and socially developed practices generate genuine purposes and discoverable or improvable values without top-down design.
Establish that autonomy, self-control, reasoning, and robust abilities ground responsibility even if underlying processes are deterministic, while indeterminacy supplies no added control.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve indispensable personal-level explanations of meaning, love, beauty, and agency while denying that explanatory autonomy entails metaphysical irreducibility.
Ground confidence in further naturalistic explanation in its empirical record and explanatory economy rather than an unsupported promise of completeness.

sections.title: Consciousness and Physical Description
sections.rationale: Tests whether experience is ontologically basic or an additional fact beyond physical description, against accounts based on unconscious computation, neural responsiveness, functional capacities, and the rejection of an inner show.

sections.title: Personal Identity, the Self, and Continuity
sections.rationale: Addresses whether memory, anticipation, unified awareness, embodiment, and informational continuity require a persisting nonphysical subject or can be explained by an evolved self-model and materially realized organization.

sections.title: Purpose, Intentionality, and Future Direction
sections.rationale: Examines whether future-directed thought and action possess irreducible aboutness and causal efficacy or arise through natural selection, predictive processing, and organized goal-directed capacities.

sections.title: Value, Meaning, and Higher-Level Explanation
sections.rationale: Determines whether objective obligation, beauty, love, and meaningful conduct require realities beyond a physical catalogue or remain genuine through evolved practices and autonomous higher-level explanations.

sections.title: Freedom, Agency, and Responsibility
sections.rationale: Compares libertarian control by a deciding self with compatibilist autonomy and robust abilities, including whether alternative futures are required for culpability and whether indeterminacy adds control rather than randomness.

sections.title: Reduction, Causation, and Explanatory Scope
sections.rationale: Assesses substrate dependence, brain access versus production, causal and functional sufficiency, the conceptual boundary of the physical, and the evidential warrant for expecting naturalistic explanation to cover the full motion.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Consciousness is ontologically prior, while the material world is constructed from conscious experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly invites Keith to define idealism, and the uninterrupted answer presents his first-person account.

response.rationale: This constructive move states Ward's motion-level idealist thesis that consciousness is ontologically basic and matter is constructed from experience.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly establishes the proposed ontology but gives only compressed support for the construction claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: The ontological-priority claim is recoverable, but the sense in which matter is constructed from consciousness remains only partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A sweeping ontological conclusion is asserted from a brief idealist formulation without defending the inference from experienced data to all material reality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The thesis is internally intelligible, but the bridge from conscious perception to the construction and ontological dependence of matter is materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cited idealist account illustrates the position but does not independently establish that consciousness constitutes the material world.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the motion bridge by asserting an ontological basis beyond an exhaustive physical inventory.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily advances its own ontology and does not meaningfully interpret a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly calls consciousness prior and describes the material world as a construction from consciousness, while supplying mainly an idealist example.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Scientific investigation indicates that conscious experience depends on complex unconscious computations in the brain, reversing the claim that experience is ontologically prior to the physical world.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly asks Daniel for the naturalist account, and the ensuing sustained answer directly contrasts Keith's position.

components.text: Whether conscious experience is ontologically prior to the physical processes investigated by science.

response.rationale: The reply directly counters priority by claiming that ordinary conscious experience depends on sophisticated unconscious brain computation, though dependence alone does not settle constitution.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the central priority claim, but leaves the dependence-to-ontology inference only partially defended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The dependence claim and its intended reversal are clear, with an implicit limitation to scientifically investigated human experience.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Scientific dependence is plausibly asserted, but treating it as an outright reversal of idealist ontology modestly exceeds the stated evidence.

charity.alternative: Epistemic priority of experience may coexist with its causal dependence on unconscious neural processing.
charity.decisiveQualification: Neural dependence by itself does not establish that experience is ontologically reducible to neural computation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dependence argument is coherent, but it needs a further bridge from computational dependence to the rejection of ontological priority.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The appeal to scientific investigation is relevant and plausible, yet no representative finding or competing interpretation is developed in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports the brain-based consciousness bridge by grounding experience in unconscious neural computation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately challenges untutored experiential authority but only partly distinguishes epistemic priority from ontological priority.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says untutored waking experience turns out to depend on complex and sophisticated unconscious computations occurring in the brain.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Conscious awareness is an additional fact beyond any complete physical description because first-person experience remains directly known even while particular mental judgments can be fallible.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator names Keith and requests his objection; Ward then gives a sustained first-person response about brains and awareness.

components.text: Whether neural computational dependence exhausts the fact of directly known conscious awareness.

response.rationale: Ward contacts the computational account by distinguishing fallible judgments from directly known awareness and asserting that awareness remains additional to physical description.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly identifies the alleged explanatory remainder, though it does not fully show why direct knowledge entails nonphysical constitution.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly separates awareness from particular fallible judgments and explicitly limits direct access to one's own consciousness.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The certainty of being aware is carefully qualified, but the further claim that awareness is additional to every physical description remains underwarranted.

charity.alternative: A physicalist can accept direct first-person knowledge while holding that its object is physically realized.
charity.decisiveQualification: Epistemic immediacy does not alone establish ontological addition or irreducibility.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The introspective premise is coherent, but the inference from direct awareness to an additional nonphysical fact remains a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: First-person awareness supports the phenomenological premise, while the claim about completeness of physical description receives no independent demonstration.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central conscious-experience bridge by identifying awareness as a fact allegedly unexhausted by physical description.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly concedes fallibility and other-mind limits, but does not fully answer the epistemic-to-ontological distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly concedes fallibility and lack of direct access to other minds while asserting direct knowledge of awareness beyond physical description.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Positing consciousness beyond observable cognitive capacities repeats the discarded vitalist demand for an extra property beyond the processes that constitute life.
moves.attributionBasis: Following the moderator's request for a response, Dennett identifies Chalmers's formulation and argues against it in his own voice.

components.text: Whether an extra fact of consciousness must be added beyond all observable cognitive capacities.
Whether consciousness must be treated as an ontologically additional basis rather than a constituted capacity.

response.rationale: Dennett diagnoses the demand for an extra consciousness property as repeating vitalism and states that the proposed addition is detached from the capacities being explained.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply expressly attacks the extra-property inference, although the analogy does not independently prove that phenomenal experience is exhausted by capacities.

precisionFindings.rationale: The vitalism comparison is recoverable, but the precise boundary between consciousness itself and studied conscious capacities remains partly unstable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The analogy supplies a plausible diagnostic warning, but the suggestion that the two explanatory demands are equivalent is stronger than the excerpt establishes.

charity.alternative: The phenomenal remainder may differ from vital force because it identifies first-person character rather than a duplicate causal mechanism.
charity.decisiveQualification: An analogy to vitalism must show relevant parity, not merely that both positions posit something extra.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The diagnostic analogy is coherent, but its force depends on an underdefended equivalence between life-process completeness and consciousness-capacity completeness.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The historical comparison is suggestive rather than demonstrative and offers little specific support that all relevant conscious facts track the studied capacities.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the central conscious-experience bridge by rejecting the need for a phenomenal addition beyond functional capacities.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response identifies the extra-property structure but materially compresses the strongest disanalogy concerning first-person phenomenology.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly calls the extra-consciousness proposal a renewed vitalist mistake and says it is disconnected from the capacities Dennett studies.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: The brain provides access to consciousness rather than producing it, so impaired neural retrieval need not establish that memories or consciousness have ceased to exist.
moves.attributionBasis: Ward begins with explicit disagreement and states his access model, including a clearly marked first-person conclusion about memory.

components.text: Whether neural dependence should be interpreted as production of consciousness rather than access to it.
Whether an access model supplies a coherent extra-consciousness alternative to functional production.

response.rationale: The access model directly contests the interpretation of brain dependence, but it does not answer the vitalism diagnostic or support the survival of inaccessible memories.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive production-versus-access issue but leaves the competing diagnostic and empirical discrimination substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The access thesis is stated clearly as Ward's view, and the Alzheimer's example makes its intended scope readily recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Ward marks the claim as his belief, but continued existence of inaccessible memories is asserted without evidence distinguishing access failure from loss.

charity.alternative: Neural impairment may alter consciousness because the brain realizes or produces memory rather than merely retrieving it.
charity.decisiveQualification: An access model needs discriminating evidence beyond compatibility with observed impairment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The access model is possible and internally intelligible, but the persistence conclusion does not follow from retrieval failure without an additional premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Alzheimer's case is compatible with the proposal but provides no verification that memories continue to exist outside retrievable neural realization.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary access-not-production bridge through an explicit alternative interpretation of neural impairment.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges neural effects but does not seriously compare production and access models against the same observations.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ward calls the brain an access machine and uses Alzheimer's retrieval failure to assert that memories continue despite loss of brain access.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Memory, anticipation, and the ownership of experience require a persisting subject that is embodied and uses the brain but is not identical with it.
moves.attributionBasis: After the moderator asks Ward about the soul, Ward gives an extended account of the subject that possesses temporally linked experiences.

components.text: Whether unconscious brain computation can constitute temporally unified ownership, memory, and anticipation.
Whether positing a persisting subject adds an unnecessary entity beyond cognitive capacities.

response.rationale: The move supplies a contrary subject-based account of temporal ownership but does not examine how computation might realize continuity or answer the redundancy objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is issue-bearing contrary material, yet it largely restates the need for a subject instead of contacting the opposing explanatory mechanism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The continuing subject thesis is clear, though the exact ontological nature and persistence conditions of that subject remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The argument treats possession and temporal linkage as requiring a non-brain subject without excluding process, organism, or self-model accounts.

charity.alternative: A temporally organized brain or organism could be the subject that owns linked experiences without a separate entity.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing that experiences need a bearer does not establish that the bearer is not the brain or organism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from linked experiences to some subject is understandable, but the further nonidentity conclusion is largely asserted and risks begging the question.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Memory and anticipation motivate continuity, yet no evidence discriminates a nonphysical persisting subject from materially organized continuity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central persisting-agent-subject bridge by arguing that temporal experience requires a continuing owner.

representationalCharity.rationale: Ward briefly names the brain alternative but rejects it without addressing its strongest account of diachronic organization.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt infers a subject from linked memories and possessed experiences, then explicitly rejects the brain or part of the brain as that subject.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Consciousness and the apparent self function as an evolved user interface that simplifies internal and external complexity without requiring a separate inner user.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks who uses the brain, and Dennett immediately answers that the brain is its own user before developing the interface model.

components.text: Whether using the brain requires a separate persisting inner subject that serves as its user.
Whether consciousness includes an additional fact beyond evolved functional organization.
Whether the brain is merely an access device used by consciousness.

response.rationale: Dennett answers that the brain is its own user and offers an evolved interface model, thereby contacting the separate-user, additional-fact, and access-machine claims.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply directly replaces the inner user with a functional model, though it compresses how the interface yields unified first-person experience.

precisionFindings.rationale: The functional thesis is clear, but calling consciousness a user illusion risks instability between denying consciousness and denying an inner presentation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Evolutionary interface functions plausibly answer the user question, but the excerpt states identity with consciousness more firmly than its compressed mechanism warrants.

charity.alternative: The pro position may posit an embodied subject, not a homuncular inner observer viewing a display.
charity.decisiveQualification: Defeating an inner-user regress does not by itself defeat every account of a persisting embodied subject.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The self-using system and interface analogy are coherent, while the bridge from useful self-model to the full apparent subject remains materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Computer-interface functionality supplies a helpful model, but the evolutionary and learning claims are asserted without representative empirical support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central brain-based consciousness and self bridge by replacing a separate user with evolved organization.

representationalCharity.rationale: The interface model is relevant and avoids a homunculus, but it partially assimilates the opposing subject to an inner computer user.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes consciousness as an effective user illusion designed by evolution, learning, and culture to make brains behaviorally capable.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: A wholly physical account cannot preserve genuine purpose because physical laws and atomic processes have no purposes of their own, making experienced aims merely illusory.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly challenges the preceding naturalistic account and consistently presents Ward's first-person objection to physical causation.

components.text: Whether a brain described as an evolved interface can possess genuine purposes rather than merely simulate them.
Whether purposeless neural and physical processes can preserve experienced aims as causally genuine.
Whether functional capacities exhaust the purposive features attributed to conscious agents.

response.rationale: Ward directly challenges the interface and physical accounts on purpose, arguing that purposeless laws and atoms cannot ground genuine aims, while leaving the functional-capacity reply undeveloped.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive purpose issue is contacted, but the move assumes rather than demonstrates that purposeless components cannot compose purposive systems.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is recoverable, but purpose shifts between intrinsic purpose of components and genuine system-level goal direction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion that physicalism loses purpose is stated categorically without addressing emergence, organization, or relational functional purpose.

charity.alternative: Purposeless laws and atoms may compose evolved systems with genuine system-level goals and control capacities.
charity.decisiveQualification: Absence of purpose in components does not entail absence of purpose in the organized whole.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reasoning relies on a composition inference from purposeless basic processes to purposeless organized agents without defending that inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The purposelessness of physical laws is relevant, but no evidence or mechanism comparison supports the claim that organized brains cannot have purposes.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the central naturalistic purpose bridge by alleging that physical processes cannot preserve genuine purposive agency.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument materially weakens the naturalistic alternative by treating component-level purposelessness as decisive against emergent system-level purpose.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt stresses that atoms and physical laws lack purposes and concludes that purpose would become merely part of an inner illusion.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Natural selection is a purposeless physical process that gradually creates genuine purposes in organisms, limbs, eyes, and tools without a top-down divine purpose giver.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly invokes Dennett's book and gives his characteristic Darwinian bottom-up explanation of purpose.

components.text: Whether a purposeless physical process can generate genuine purposes at the level of organisms and artifacts.

response.rationale: Dennett squarely answers the composition objection by identifying natural selection as a bottom-up process that creates purposes in organisms, organs, and tools.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive premise and supplies a clear alternative generative direction from purposeless selection to purposive organization.

precisionFindings.rationale: The bottom-up claim and examples are clear, with an implicit restriction to evolved and culturally derived functional purposes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The evolutionary origin of biological functions is well fitted, though calling all listed purposes genuine without defining normativity slightly exceeds the excerpt's warrant.

charity.alternative: The objection concerns conscious or normative purpose, not merely biological and artifact function.
charity.decisiveQualification: An evolutionary function account must bridge from selected effects to experienced, reason-guided purposes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The bottom-up generative inference is coherent and directly avoids the composition fallacy, with one bounded bridge from evolved function to conscious purpose.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Natural selection and the organ examples provide representative support, but the transition to human purposes and normative aims is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central emergent-purpose bridge by explaining how purposeless selection generates organized functions and aims.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply handles the component-to-system challenge strongly but only partially addresses the distinction between function and conscious purpose.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly identifies natural selection as a purposeless process that produces purposes in agents, tools, limbs, and eyes from the bottom up.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Future-directed intentionality resists physical reduction because a present idea can refer to a nonexistent future outcome and causally guide action toward realizing it.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained first-person argument follows Ward's stated rejection of Dennett's project and develops his intentionality objection.

components.text: Whether evolutionary organization can explain present representations that guide action toward future outcomes.
Whether an evolved interface can possess causally efficacious future-directed representations.

response.rationale: Ward raises a genuine intentionality challenge and contacts the interface account, but he does not address selection's capacity to produce predictive, future-directed control structures.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move is relevant and contacts a secondary functional issue, while leaving the primary Darwinian generative explanation largely unexamined.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal role of a present future-representation is clear, but the scope shifts between irreducible reference and any physical description of predictive behavior.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The explanatory question is forceful, but treating reference to a nonexistent future as resistant to all physical accounts outruns the supplied argument.

charity.alternative: A current neural representation can encode predicted future states and causally guide action without the future state acting backward.
charity.decisiveQualification: The relevant cause may be the present representation, not the nonexistent future object itself.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The phenomenon is clearly identified, but the argument equivocates between causation by a present representation and causation by its future referent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ordinary goal-directed action supports the premise, while no evidence excludes predictive physical representations as its causal mechanism.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central purpose-value-freedom bridge by arguing for irreducible intentional content and causal efficacy.

representationalCharity.rationale: Ward notices the present idea's causal role but does not engage the strongest representational distinction between content and causal vehicle.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks how a present thought can refer to a nonexistent future outcome and emphasizes that the present idea appears to guide realization of that outcome.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Objective moral obligations are discovered rather than invented, and their connection to purpose and agency places value outside an exhaustive physical catalogue.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted turn uses Ward's first-person commitments and develops his linked account of value, agency, and the subject self.

response.rationale: This constructive move links discovered moral obligations, purposive agency, and value outside a physical catalogue to the motion-level irreducibility claim.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves it advances a major independent route, but compresses the bridge from objective obligation to nonphysical ontology.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claims about discovery, obligation, value, purpose, and agency are recoverable, though objective status is not further analyzed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Objective obligation and exclusion from a physical catalogue are asserted categorically without defending moral realism or excluding naturalistic realism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The linkage among value, purpose, and agency is coherent, but the move leaves a material inference from objectivity to nonphysical irreducibility.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The existence of experienced obligation supplies intuitive support, while discovery and nonphysical status remain substantially asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move supports the motion bridge by presenting objective value and obligation as realities outside an exhaustive physical catalogue.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move constructs Ward's positive value argument without interpreting a developed opposing alternative in this span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls moral obligations truths about the universe, says value is not part of a physical catalogue, and connects value with purpose and agency.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Humanly constructed systems can contain discoverable constraints and opportunities for improvement, so evolved moral practices may support genuine moral discovery without requiring values external to nature.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn explicitly identifies Ward's position before answering through Darwinian predictive coding, chess, and cultural moral development.

components.text: Whether genuine moral discovery requires values that exist independently of human construction and nature.
Whether evolved predictive capacities can generate discoveries and improve goal-directed practices.

response.rationale: Dennett directly contests the discovery-versus-construction inference through chess and evolved moral practice, while also invoking predictive and cultural development.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive inference with a clear counterexample, though it does not fully establish the objectivity or authority of moral constraints.

precisionFindings.rationale: The compatibility of construction with discovery is clearly stated, with the moral extension implicitly qualified as evolutionary and cultural.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The chess analogy warrants the compatibility claim, and the broader moral conclusion is presented as an available evolutionary account rather than certainty.

charity.alternative: Objective moral obligations may demand stronger authority than discoveries internal to a constructed game.
charity.decisiveQualification: Chess establishes construction-discovery compatibility but not that moral normativity is merely system-internal.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample coherently defeats a simple construction-versus-discovery dichotomy, with one bounded gap in extending the analogy to moral authority.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Chess supplies a concrete counterexample and cultural evolution supplies a plausible model, but representative moral evidence and rival comparison are limited.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports emergent value by showing how constructed and evolved systems can contain discoverable, improvable constraints.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly targets the inference from discovery to external existence, while leaving the strongest authority disanalogy partly unanswered.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt uses chess as a human construction that nonetheless contains surprising discoveries, then extends that compatibility to evolved moral codes.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Responsibility-relevant freedom consists in autonomy, self-control, and robust practical abilities, none of which requires the underlying physical world to be indeterministic.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett explicitly presents the compatibilist view, using autonomous systems, self-control, and the putting example to define relevant freedom.

components.text: Whether responsibility and agency require a nonphysical value-bearing chooser rather than autonomous control capacities.
Whether physically realized systems can possess genuine goal-directed control and purposes.
Whether practical abilities can guide future-directed conduct without indeterministic causation.

response.rationale: Dennett justifies replacing metaphysical indeterminism with the responsibility-relevant demand for autonomy, self-control, and robust abilities, preserving the practical agency issue.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe preserves control and responsibility while directly identifying the functional capacities that allegedly do the required work.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move distinguishes relevant varieties of freedom and clearly specifies autonomy, control, and robust practical ability as its scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is firmly advocated but appropriately tied to responsibility-relevant freedom, not every conceivable definition of metaphysical freedom.

charity.alternative: Libertarian freedom demands ultimate alternative possibilities, not merely autonomous abilities within a determined history.
charity.decisiveQualification: A compatibilist reframe must explain why robust control satisfies responsibility despite the absence of ultimate alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The functional account is consistent and avoids dependence on indeterminism, with one bounded implicit bridge from robust ability to full moral responsibility.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Autonomous systems, control contrasts, and practical examples support the account, though broader responsibility evidence and rival cases are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central compatible-agency bridge by grounding relevant freedom in autonomy, self-control, and robust abilities.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately distinguishes the rival demand and offers a substantive replacement, though the responsibility bridge is somewhat compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes autonomous from externally controlled systems and argues that practical varieties of freedom do not depend on determinism being false.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Libertarian freedom requires genuinely alternative futures under an agent's control, grounding culpability because the person need not have performed the wrongful act.
moves.attributionBasis: Ward identifies himself as a libertarian and develops the view through alternative futures, legal guilt, moral culpability, and Humean doubt.

components.text: Whether autonomy and robust abilities suffice for culpability without genuinely open alternative futures.

response.rationale: Ward directly contests the compatibilist criterion by requiring alternative futures under the person's control and linking that capacity to moral culpability.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive sufficiency claim, but largely states the libertarian requirement rather than demonstrating why compatibilist control cannot ground culpability.

precisionFindings.rationale: The libertarian requirement is explicitly identified, and the thought-experiment qualification makes the alternative-futures claim recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity of controlled alternatives for culpability is asserted with a clear rationale, but competing responsibility conditions are not fully excluded.

charity.alternative: Compatibilist responsibility may depend on reasons-responsive abilities across nearby situations, not a different outcome under an identical past.
charity.decisiveQualification: A rewind test is not the only coherent account of robust alternative ability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The controlled-alternatives account is internally coherent, though the inference from culpability to identical-past alternatives remains a material disputed bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Legal and moral intuitions support the demand, but no evidence or case comparison establishes that compatibilist abilities are insufficient.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central compatible-agency bridge by denying that autonomy alone supplies responsibility-relevant freedom.

representationalCharity.rationale: Ward squarely distinguishes his view but does not fully engage the strongest modal and reasons-responsive compatibilist account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly requires alternative possible futures under the agent's control and presents this difference as central to libertarian freedom.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: An agent self can decide among courses of action while upbringing, education, character, and habits influence choices without fully determining the decision made.
moves.attributionBasis: Ward contrasts deciding with merely finding oneself acting and explicitly identifies the subject self as an agent traditionally called the soul.

components.text: Whether character, education, and prior causes determine action or merely influence a deciding agent.
Whether acquired moral practices can shape choice without exhausting personal agency.

response.rationale: Ward directly distinguishes influence from determination and locates decision in an agent self, thereby answering the compatibilist emphasis on formed capacities and character.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move directly contacts causal determination, but supplies little account of how the agent decision operates without determination or randomness.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between causal influence and full determination is explicit, and the agent-self claim has a clear limited target.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Influence without determination is presented coherently, but the existence and causal role of the undetermined self exceed the evidence supplied.

charity.alternative: A determined choice may still be the agent's own when it flows through character, reasons, and self-control.
charity.decisiveQualification: Contrasting decision with compulsion does not establish that authentic decision must be undetermined.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The influence-versus-determination distinction is coherent, but the positive causal model of agent selection remains a material unexplained bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: First-person decision language and ordinary causal distinctions provide some support, while no discriminating evidence establishes agent-causal indeterminism.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central purpose-value-freedom bridge through a deciding agent whose choices are influenced but not determined.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes character and education as influences but insufficiently engages ownership under reasons-responsive determination.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts a present act of deciding with prior upbringing and education, which Ward treats as influential rather than determining conditions.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Adding genuine physical indeterminacy to an otherwise identical agent contributes randomness rather than greater control, trustworthiness, or responsibility.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett introduces the contrasting robot-babysitter thought experiment and draws the explicit conclusion that indeterminacy amounts to randomness.

components.text: Whether removing determination adds agent control rather than an uncontrolled random difference.
Whether genuine alternative futures produced by indeterminacy increase responsibility or trustworthiness.

response.rationale: The matched-robot thought experiment expressly diagnoses bare indeterminacy as randomness and states that it supplies no reason to prefer the undetermined agent.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly attacks the decisive control inference and tests the alleged benefit of indeterminacy in an otherwise matched comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is clearly limited to adding genuine random indeterminacy to an otherwise identical control architecture.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Within the stipulated matched case, the conclusion that random variation adds no control is proportionate to the thought experiment.

charity.alternative: Libertarian agency may involve agent causation, not merely insertion of a random physical event.
charity.decisiveQualification: Refuting bare event randomness does not by itself refute a developed agent-causal mechanism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The controlled comparison clearly shows that replacing pseudorandomness with genuine randomness does not add the relevant kind of control.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The thought experiment provides strong conceptual support, though it does not empirically test or exhaust every agent-causal libertarian proposal.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central compatible-agency bridge by showing that indeterminacy alone contributes no responsibility-enhancing control.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument strongly defeats indeterminacy alone, but only partially reaches the strongest claim that a self controls which alternative occurs.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts otherwise matched robot carers differing only in genuine versus pseudorandom variation and asks why the indeterminate one should be trusted more.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Reproducibility and practical immortality alter the force of promises, threats, and punishment, showing that ordinary moral personhood depends materially on mortality and vulnerability.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained argument uses Dennett's characteristic robot comparison and is immediately addressed by Ward as Dennett's preceding claim.

components.text: Whether personal continuity requires a persisting subject rather than materially vulnerable organization.
Whether moral agency depends on a continuing chooser beyond reproducible physical information.

response.rationale: The mortality argument bears on embodied personhood but does not directly answer the continuing-subject inference or the causal account of agent choice.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It offers relevant contrary material about vulnerability while leaving both identified decisive metaphysical demands uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The moral importance of mortality is recoverable, but the jump from robot reproducibility to contracts and personhood is textually compressed and unstable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical advice against contracting with robots and the personhood conclusion exceed what mortality and reproducibility alone establish.

charity.alternative: A reproducible artificial agent might remain accountable through institutional identity, assets, commitments, and continuity rules.
charity.decisiveQualification: Reduced vulnerability changes enforcement incentives but does not automatically eliminate agency or contractual identity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Mortality plausibly affects threats and punishment, but the inference to nonpersonhood or invalid promises contains substantial unsupported steps.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The robot comparison is illustrative, while no representative evidence establishes that mortality and fragility are necessary conditions of personhood.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the central persisting-subject bridge by emphasizing materially grounded vulnerability, though the contact is indirect within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move highlights a real practical difference but materially understates ways responsibility could survive reproducibility.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt connects robot reproducibility or practical immortality with weakened contracts and concludes that robots lack personhood because they are not fragile or mortal.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Possessing an informational encoding is insufficient for continued personal existence because stored structure must be concretely realized before the conscious or meaningful entity exists.
moves.attributionBasis: The Beethoven analogy advances Ward's recurring distinction between abstract information and an actually realized, experienced subject or work.

components.text: Whether stored or reproducible information is sufficient for continued existence of the person or meaningful work.
Whether informational organization alone constitutes the experienced subject.

response.rationale: The Beethoven analogy directly distinguishes an encoding from its realized, hearable instance and applies that distinction to informational accounts of survival.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the information-versus-realization issue, but only analogically addresses personal consciousness and does not resolve identity across realizations.

precisionFindings.rationale: The encoding-realization distinction is clear, but its extension from musical works to personal survival is only implicit in the short span.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that encoding requires realization for audible existence is warranted, while the personal-survival extension remains implicitly qualified.

charity.alternative: An informational continuity theory need not claim that an uninstantiated encoding is presently conscious; it may require later realization.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy defeats bare storage sufficiency but not survival through appropriately continuous re-instantiation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy supports the need for realization, with a material but bounded bridge from musical performance to conscious personal identity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Beethoven example clearly illustrates the conceptual distinction, but offers little independent evidence about survival of conscious persons.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the central persisting-subject bridge by denying that abstract informational encoding alone constitutes continued personal existence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly distinguishes information from realization but does not address the strongest realized-copy account of continuity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says digital musical information is not sufficient for the symphony's realized existence because it still must be converted into something hearable.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Purpose, beauty, joy, love, promising, mortality, and the desire for immortality can receive naturalistic explanations without losing their importance or wonder.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly contrasts Dennett's naturalism with Ward's idealism, and this answer states the naturalist position in the first person plural.

components.text: Whether naturalistic explanation necessarily eliminates genuine value, meaning, beauty, love, and wonder.
Whether naturalistic explanation can preserve genuine purpose rather than declare it illusory.
Whether naturalistic explanation preserves responsibility-relevant human significance.
Whether naturalism can explain mortality and the desire for immortality without reducing their importance.

response.rationale: Dennett directly denies that naturalistic accounts diminish purpose and value, and includes mortality and immortality, but mainly asserts adequacy rather than displaying the accounts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts several decisive preservation demands, while the explanatory mechanisms and the freedom component remain substantially undeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The preservation thesis and its list of phenomena are clear, with adequacy implicitly limited to available or developing naturalistic accounts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that all listed phenomena have adequate naturalistic accounts is much stronger than the unelaborated catalogue establishes.

charity.alternative: The opposing concern is explanatory and ontological adequacy, not merely whether naturalists continue to feel wonder.
charity.decisiveQualification: Preserving appreciation does not demonstrate that naturalism fully explains objective value or conscious meaning.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Naturalistic explanation and retained wonder are compatible, but compatibility does not establish explanatory adequacy for every listed phenomenon.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The broad list identifies relevant explananda, while no specific account, evidence, or comparison supports the asserted adequacy in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the motion-level naturalistic-sufficiency bridge by expressly claiming preservation and explanation across most motion phenomena.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly rejects an eliminativist consequence but partially substitutes preservation of wonder for the stronger irreducibility challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt lists purpose, beauty, joy, love, promising, death, and immortality as naturally explicable without diminishing life's wonderfulness.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Naturalism remains an unfinished explanatory program, so confidence that it will ultimately describe every disputed feature of persons is a substantive commitment rather than an established result.
moves.attributionBasis: Ward poses a clearly adversarial follow-up that characterizes the acknowledged incompleteness of Dennett's naturalistic project as faith.

components.text: Whether the asserted adequacy of naturalistic accounts is already established or remains unfinished work.
Whether the naturalistic consciousness program is complete enough to warrant its comprehensive claims.
Whether evolutionary explanation already covers every disputed aspect of purpose.

response.rationale: Ward elicits agreement that the project is incomplete and then directly questions whether confidence in eventual comprehensiveness is a substantive faith commitment.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The exchange sharply contacts the gap between present incompleteness and future confidence, though the term faith carries an underargued evidential implication.

precisionFindings.rationale: The unfinished-project question is clear, but faith is unstable between unsupported belief and ordinary evidence-based confidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately poses a challenge rather than claiming that incompleteness disproves naturalism, and it explicitly establishes the work-in-progress premise.

charity.alternative: Confidence in an unfinished program may be inductive and evidence-based rather than unsupported faith.
charity.decisiveQualification: Acknowledged incompleteness does not by itself show that projected explanatory success is unwarranted.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The challenge coherently distinguishes completed explanation from confidence in future completion, without claiming that incompleteness alone refutes naturalism.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Dennett's express agreement that work remains supplies direct support, though the stronger implication about evidential warrant remains unresolved.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary limits-of-naturalistic-completeness bridge by testing confidence in an admittedly unfinished program.

representationalCharity.rationale: The question legitimately exposes incompleteness, but the faith framing only partly accommodates evidence-based methodological trust.

moves.evidenceBasis: The exchange records agreement that completion remains future work and asks whether confidence that naturalism will describe everything therefore constitutes faith.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Confidence in continued naturalistic explanation is evidence-based practical trust in a method with a record of success, comparable to ordinary reliance on engineering.
moves.attributionBasis: This is Dennett's immediate first-person answer to Ward's question and explicitly grounds his confidence in accumulated practical evidence.

components.text: Whether confidence in future naturalistic explanation is unsupported faith or evidence-based methodological trust.

response.rationale: Dennett immediately answers the faith challenge by distinguishing evidence-based reliance from unsupported belief through the ordinary engineering comparison.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive evidential issue, although the analogy does not establish the naturalistic program's domain-specific success rate.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between evidence-based trust and unsupported faith is clear, with the confidence implicitly inductive rather than certain.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The practical-trust analogy asserts warranted confidence rather than certainty and is proportionate to the limited methodological conclusion.

charity.alternative: Engineering trust may rest on mature quantified performance unlike prediction of complete naturalistic explanation across disputed phenomena.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy needs domain-specific evidence before equal confidence is warranted.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inductive distinction is coherent, though the analogy needs a bounded bridge showing comparable evidence and reliability across the relevant domains.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ordinary engineering reliability illustrates evidence-based trust, but the excerpt does not identify the naturalistic track record relevant to every disputed phenomenon.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary evidence-based-method bridge by grounding confidence in accumulated evidence rather than mere promise.

representationalCharity.rationale: The answer fairly addresses evidential trust but leaves a significant disanalogy between bridge reliability and comprehensive explanatory projection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares naturalistic confidence to ordinary confidence in engineered bridges and explicitly characterizes that faith as based on evidence.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Higher-level explanations cannot be replaced by descriptions of atoms and electrons, but their explanatory autonomy does not make their subjects metaphysically irreducible.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett answers the reductionism objection through a sustained levels-of-explanation argument illustrated by the economic value of currency.

components.text: Whether failure of microphysical description to replace higher-level explanation demonstrates metaphysical irreducibility.
Whether absence of value terms from an atomic catalogue places value outside natural reality.
Whether purposive explanation at a higher level requires purposive fundamental components.
Whether nonreplaceability by a physical description entails an additional nonphysical fact.

response.rationale: Dennett diagnoses an inference from explanatory-level autonomy to metaphysical irreducibility and uses economic value to state the defeating consequence that the levels can coexist naturally.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive inference shared by several pro moves and supplies a clear counterexample to equating nonreplacement with nonphysicality.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between explanatory nonreplaceability and metaphysical irreducibility is explicit, stable, and illustrated at a clearly specified level.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited conclusion that level autonomy does not entail metaphysical irreducibility is exactly fitted to the dollar-value counterexample.

charity.alternative: Consciousness or objective normativity might resist naturalization more deeply than economic value does.
charity.decisiveQualification: The counterexample defeats the general inference but does not independently settle each domain-specific irreducibility argument.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The levels distinction is explicit and the dollar example validly shows that irreducible explanatory vocabulary need not imply nonphysical ontology.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The economic-value example strongly supports the conceptual distinction, with a bounded gap in generalizing to consciousness and objective normativity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary levels-without-dualism bridge by preserving autonomous explanation while denying metaphysical addition.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately targets a common inference and preserves higher-level reality, while acknowledging only implicitly that domains may differ.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says atomic description is the wrong level for explaining currency value and expressly denies that this explanatory fact makes dollars metaphysically irreducible.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Explanations of conduct through pursued values and a continuing deciding self capture meaningful features of life that cannot be dismissed as illusions of brain activity.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Ward directly, and the ensuing first-person statement reiterates Ward's value-centered account of action and enduring selfhood.

components.text: Whether value-directed personal explanation is fully preserved if the continuing deciding self is treated as a brain-based illusion.
Whether naturalism preserves what is most important in value-directed personal life.
Whether the continuing deciding self is merely an evolved user illusion.
Whether conduct explained by pursued value retains genuine normative significance.

response.rationale: Ward accepts value-level explanation as indispensable but directly contests the claim that its continuing subject and central importance can be ontologically deflated as illusion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the preservation and self-model issues, but relies heavily on reluctance and personal importance rather than demonstrating irreducibility.

precisionFindings.rationale: The value-directed and continuing-self claims are clear, though illusion shifts between eliminative denial and naturalistic redescriptive explanation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Ward frames the conclusion as inability to see and reluctance rather than certainty, fitting the personal-explanatory considerations actually supplied.

charity.alternative: A naturalist may regard value explanations and the continuing self-model as real higher-level patterns rather than dismissive illusions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting metaphysical irreducibility need not eliminate personal-level truth or significance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Value-directed explanation and a continuing perspective are coherently linked, but their indispensability does not by itself establish a non-brain subject.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ordinary explanation by pursued values supports personal-level reality, while subjective importance and reluctance do not discriminate competing ontologies.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary levels-without-dualism bridge by arguing that higher-level value explanation requires a genuine continuing self.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes higher-level explanation but materially compresses the strongest noneliminative naturalistic interpretation of self and value.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explains conduct through values and says neither life's central values nor the continuing deciding self can plausibly be dismissed as mere brain illusion.
